episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Science, Wonder & the Natural World
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Science, Wonder & the Natural World.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: Who gets to call themselves local?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down Pile burning throughout the Chilcotin until end of January and Downtown Trick r Treat returns in Williams Lake, plus 14 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: Does long-term, documented field observation of a place earn its keepers a meaningful say in decisions about that place, or does decision authority belong to the people who live beside it? Topics include: Credibility of long-term observational records versus who bears decision costs, El Niño forecasting, regional impacts, and headline overstatement, Peer review and disclosure in the heat-mortality estimate, Custody and standing of local monitoring records (Cow Moose Sign Project, Helen Sandy photographs, fossil and meteorite provenance), Dementia and daylight exposure association in wrist-device data.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: South Cariboo Sustainability Society

discussion.central_question: Does long-term, documented field observation of a place earn its keepers a meaningful say in decisions about that place, or does decision authority belong to the people who live beside it?
discussion.riley_position: Twenty years of repeated observation is rare and earns a voice; a credible record should carry weight in decisions because it provides the baseline and lead time planners need, even if the record-holder should not be the one who decides.
riley_key_evidence: NOAA's Climate Prediction Center put the chance of strong-to-very-strong El Niño through January to March 2027 above 83 per cent, with an earlier 63 per cent chance of sea surface temperatures passing 2.0 degrees.
Lonnie Thompson's Guliya Plateau ice cores drilled in 1992 and 2015 showed matching oxygen isotope patterns, demonstrating reproducibility through return visits.
The Climate Impact Lab's model draws on more than 24,000 regional temperature-mortality relationships and is useful for ranking where heat response is needed first.
discussion.casey_position: Monitors bring evidence to the room but should not set the agenda or answer for outcomes; local people who bear the costs should decide, and claims built on headline figures or unclear custody of records should be challenged.
casey_key_evidence: The University of Chicago estimate moved from about 451,000 excess heat deaths to roughly 857,000 total, with coverage rounding to 870,000 or nearly 900,000, and the work had not been peer-reviewed.

Researchers followed 87,577 adults wearing wrist light devices over a median of 8.1 years, with 741 dementia cases; the association (16 per cent lower risk above 1,000 lux) does not prove daylight prevents dementia.
Helen Sandy spent twenty years photographing Indigenous fishing camps in Farwell Canyon, and the Teghaza meteorite study's claims rest on a custody chain no one publishes.
discussion.resolution: They did not fully agree: Riley would give the record-holder a seat at the table while Casey would keep record-holders from setting the agenda, and Casey explicitly asked to leave that point open. They converged on the practical step of writing down custody and the list of who was consulted for a chosen local record.

research.block:
PRE-RESEARCHED INSIGHTS FOR THE DEEP DIVE

RESEARCH QUESTION: How strong is the 2026-27 El Niño forecast, and how confident are the agencies issuing it?

Findings: NOAA's Climate Prediction Center says El Niño is present, is strengthening, and is likely to be strong-to-very strong through January–March 2027, with more than an 83% chance of that. An earlier NOAA update put the chance of sea surface temperatures exceeding 2.0°C at 63%. A USA Today report from 13 August 2026 said federal scientists gave a greater-than-90% chance of a "very strong" event in fall and winter 2026-27. The WMO's 3 September update projected a peak toward the end of 2026. Forecast probabilities have been rising over the summer, which matters for how much weight to give any single headline.
Sources: NOAA CPC ENSO Diagnostic Discussion (cpc.ncep.noaa.gov); NOAA news release "El Niño forms, expected to strengthen"; USA Today, 13 Aug 2026; elninolive.com tracker.
Suggested angle: Riley can argue this is a success story for forecasting: models flagged the event months ahead, giving countries time to prepare. Casey can push back that a probability is not a certainty, and that "forecast among the strongest on record" depends on the index and the lead time. Both can agree the signal is strong enough to take seriously, and disagree about whether forecasts of this kind translate into action.

RESEARCH QUESTION: Is the "870,000 deaths" figure a settled finding?

Findings: The figure comes from the University of Chicago's Climate Impact Lab El Niño Heat Mortality Tracker. The headline number has been revised upward over time. The first estimate was about 451,000 excess heat deaths between June 2026 and February 2027. A later update, with data through March, projected about 857,000 total deaths, with roughly 373,000 in the following six months. Press coverage has rounded this to 870,000 or "nearly 900,000." The estimate has not yet been peer-reviewed, although the team says it uses peer-reviewed methods, and the full method is due in an upcoming journal article. The mortality relationship is based on annual mortality data, which means it largely excludes deaths brought forward by days or weeks. One expert quoted by DW argued that most of the counted deaths would have occurred at least six months later anyway. The upward revision was attributed to hotter-than-expected August and September temperatures.
Sources: impactlab.org "451,000 at Risk"; climate.uchicago.edu "New Tracker Maps the Human Toll"; CNN (23 Sep 2026); Guardian (23 Sep 2026); DW.
Suggested angle: This is the strongest contested claim in the set. Casey can use the "deaths brought forward versus excess deaths" caveat and the non-peer-reviewed status to argue that the headline overstates the loss. Riley can respond that the modelling is built on 24,000+ regional temperature-mortality relationships and that the point is to direct heat-response resources, not to make a precise count. A good on-air question is whether a headline figure that changes by hundreds of thousands in a few months is useful for policy or just alarming.

RESEARCH QUESTION: Are the California record high tides caused by El Niño, or by something else?

Findings: The record tides were the product of several factors stacking up. The main driver was astronomical: a full moon and the moon's close approach to Earth maximised tidal pull. NOAA attributes the extra height to oceanic Kelvin waves moving north along the West Coast, which are El Niño-linked. Warmer water also expanded in volume through thermal expansion. The Los Angeles Times noted that a months-old marine heat wave, which is unrelated to El Niño, contributed as well. The Washington Post described the event as a "glimpse of sea level rise," while noting that relatively small waves limited the damage. The Guardian's account described submerged streets, homes, and disrupted train routes from San Diego to the Bay Area.
Sources: KTLA (citing NOAA); LA Times (26, 27, and 29 Oct 2026); NYT (27 Oct 2026); USA Today (26 Oct 2026); Washington Post (28 Oct 2026).
Suggested angle: This is a useful test of how we assign blame for extreme events. Casey can argue that the headline ("El Niño floods California") oversimplifies a mix of lunar cycle, ocean warming, and a separate marine heat wave, and that the sea-level-rise framing is being pushed too hard. Riley can use the same mix to show that El Niño is one link in a chain that climate science can now trace and predict. Both should agree that a single cause makes a poor story, and that the real question is how much of the extra water level is attributable to a warming baseline.
